title: Three-tier network behind a DMZ
context: Internet traffic passes provider DDoS scrubbing and a CDN, then three firewalls in turn: into the DMZ, into the app zone, into the data zone. A management VLAN collects logs.
uses: The diagram flows down, one band per zone, in the order traffic crosses them, with no layout block for the zones: the flow already stacks them. The one block is a column holding the two sources and the edge zone, which centres the sources either side of the first node they feed. Each firewall is a [bridge]: it sits on the border it guards, half in each zone, which is how network engineers draw them. [span] makes each firewall as wide as the row of nodes behind it, so every rule drops on a straight line. The nodes inside a zone are rows, not columns: with the flow running down, siblings that share a neighbour go side by side, so each has a clear drop (see docs/layout-guide.md). The SIEM is in a management zone tagged [side span]: it stands beside the stack instead of becoming a last tier, as tall as the zones it collects from, and the three firewall links cross the gutter to it.
gap: Three links into one node still arrive side by side; a bus along the gutter would join them into one line. A log link from a node in the middle of a zone, with neighbours between it and the side, would have to cross them.

title: Kubernetes ingress, service mesh and egress
context: A cloud load balancer feeds an ingress controller; services route to sidecar-injected pods across namespaces; outbound calls must leave through an egress gateway with an allow-list.
uses: Nested frames for cluster and namespaces; two titled columns side by side, so each service lines up with its pods row by row; [span] lets the ingress controller feed all three services on straight lines.
gap: The web pods call svc/cart, a link that runs backwards into the column before it. Trace draws it, but the detour is ugly, so it is left out here; a “call back” style that loops around the column edge would help.

title: Zero-trust access to internal apps
context: Users never join the network. An identity-aware proxy checks SSO, MFA and device posture on every request; an app connector inside the private network dials out, so there are no inbound ports. The legacy VPN is still there for one app.
uses: The connector is a [bridge] on the private network’s border: the picture says “this is the only way in”. proxy <- posture keeps the posture check above the flow while the arrow still points at the proxy.
gap: Trace cannot yet show “the connector dials out, then traffic flows in”. A two-headed or reversed-flow link style (arrow one way, label for the opposite connection direction) would say it better than a label.

title: Hybrid cloud: datacenter to AWS
context: An on-prem datacenter reaches an AWS VPC through a transit gateway, over Direct Connect with an IPsec VPN as backup. Public, private and database subnets; apps still authenticate against on-prem Active Directory.
uses: Four levels of nesting (region, VPC, subnet tiers) and a transit gateway as a [bridge] on the AWS border, where the datacenter link lands. tgw <- app1 sends the LDAP call back to the datacenter without turning the whole layout around. A column holds the three subnet tiers as bands inside the VPC, the way AWS reference diagrams draw them, and same-width makes the bands one width.
gap: The tiers are bands now, but the links between them (load balancer to the two app nodes, app nodes to the database) still leave and re-enter by the left side of each band.

title: Branch office LAN with dual ISPs
context: Two internet links (fiber and LTE backup), a firewall HA pair, a core switch doing inter-VLAN routing, a TLS-inspecting web proxy for staff, and four access VLANs, with guests isolated and sent straight out.
uses: Top-down, with the two ISPs and the four VLANs as titled rows; [span] stretches the core switch across all four VLANs. fw <- proxy and fw <- guest send inspected and guest traffic back up to the firewall without breaking the layering. same-width makes the edge, core and access zones one width, so the three tiers line up on both sides.
gap: The four trunks jog sideways. The layout engine keeps the core and access frames centred on each other instead of lining the switch up with the VLANs, and Trace only slides a frame back into line when nothing is in the way (here the guest bypass is). The proxy would also sit better beside the firewall, which needs a placement hint.

title: CI/CD with canary releases
context: Every commit is built and checked in parallel; green builds are signed and pushed, deployed to staging, approved, then rolled out to production through a canary that rolls back on its own if SLOs slip.
uses: [span] on the build step fans out to the three parallel checks on straight lines; red and green paths come from link tags; dev <- gate sends the failure back to the developer while keeping the pipeline flowing left to right. A column of three rows gives each stage of the pipeline its own row: CI with the developer push, then the registry and staging, then production and the rollback. It is 1,000 wide instead of 2,460, so the text stays legible when the page is fitted to a screen. align puts the registry, the deploy and test steps and the approval on one line, and the links that hop from one row to the next each use one run across.
gap: The fan-in to “all green?” converges on one point; hand-drawn pipelines often show the parallel stage as a bracket. A column could offer a “join” option that merges its outgoing links. The links from one row to the next run back to the left, because a row cannot flow right to left yet (a snake), so each hop drops and crosses back.

title: Order processing on Kafka
context: Checkout writes the order and an outbox row in one transaction; a relay publishes it; payment, inventory, shipping and notifications react to topics and publish their own events. Poison messages end in a dead-letter topic.
uses: Topics and consumers as two columns facing each other, so reading and publishing are both horizontal; tPay <- payment draws “publishes” as an arrow into the topic while the consumer stays on the right. Consumers sit beside the payment provider and dead-letter topic in a row, and the checkout API is stacked over the order service, so the diagram is not one long strip.
gap: Two crossings remain between topics and consumers; the consumer order (inventory, payment, notify, shipping) was found by trying every order. Suggesting an order automatically is part of the deferred layout recommendations.

title: Payment lifecycle
context: The states a card payment moves through, from creation to capture, refunds, voids and disputes.
uses: Start dot, rounded states, double-bordered end states and coloured paths; captured <- disputed keeps the “dispute won” loop from flipping the layout.
gap: Self-loops (another partial refund) are still small and tucked against the box. A proper loop shape with room for its label is on the list.

title: Analytics platform, sources to dashboards
context: Operational data arrives by CDC, streaming and SaaS syncs, lands in a lakehouse in bronze, silver and gold layers built by dbt, and feeds BI, ML features and reverse ETL. Airflow schedules the dbt runs; quality checks gate silver.
uses: Sources, ingestion and consumers as titled columns that line up row for row; bronze and gold are [span] nodes meeting the columns on either side; Airflow’s control links are muted so the data flow stays dominant. Airflow, the quality checks and the alert are a side zone below the pipeline ([side span]): control-plane, beside the data flow instead of in it.
gap: Without the lakehouse frame, bronze and gold line up exactly with the columns beside them; with it, the layout engine nudges the frame and the links jog.

title: Incident response
context: From an alert to a postmortem: triage, severity, paging and escalation, an incident commander, mitigation loops and status updates.
uses: Decisions as pills ending in a question mark, the happy path drawn plain, the escalation red and the dead ends muted; mitigate <- fixed draws the retry loop without the layout treating it as a new step.
gap: Close to what a careful hand would draw. The one tell is label placement on vertical links, which still takes a row of its own.

title: Microservices sharing one identity provider
context: A web and a mobile app reach seven services through a gateway; every one of them, the gateway and both apps also check a token with the same identity provider.
uses: Icons and one zone, nothing else on purpose. The eight “validate token” links to the identity provider are merged automatically into one bus: a trunk at the provider, a line past the services, a short branch from each, a dot where a branch joins, and the label written once.
gap: Merging is automatic when four or more links go to (or leave) one node with the same label and style; there is no way yet to ask for it on fewer links, or to switch it off. A branch that cannot run straight to the bus finds a free lane of its own (Orders, Catalog here), so the old detours are gone; the gateway's own fan-out, which has no labels, is still drawn as separate links.

title: Sign-in with OAuth 2.0 and PKCE
context: A single-page app signs a user in through an identity provider and then calls an API that introspects the token; the failure branch ends in an error page.
uses: Sequence mode: participants with icons, an alt/else block with a loop nested inside it, a self call, dashed replies and a note across two participants.
gap: Close to what a careful hand would draw. A self call's label wraps to two lines, and long labels on short arrows are cut to two lines rather than widening the gap.

title: Shop data model
context: Eight tables of an online shop: customers and addresses, orders and their lines, products and categories, payments and reviews.
uses: Table nodes with typed columns, key markers and a nullable column; links attach at the column and carry crow's foot cardinality; a self reference (categories) loops back on the table.
gap: Two links meet one side of Customers a few pixels apart and run side by side, and “part of” and “is a” enter Orders on the same row. Nothing tells the layout to keep tables that share many links together; a grid of tables with ordered rows would read better.

title: Engineering organisation
context: A CEO, three executives, eight departments and six teams, as an org chart.
uses: Nothing but nodes, links and icons. The four links leaving the CTO are merged into one bus automatically.
gap: A tree is drawn left to right, as the default direction says; most org charts are top-down, which `direction down` gives, but then the widest level runs off the page. Siblings are not centred on their parent.

title: Web stack in one VPC across two zones
context: A CDN and a load balancer in front of two availability zones, each with web, app and database, plus a shared cache, object storage and a NAT gateway to a payment API.
uses: `direction down`, two zones side by side in a row inside a VPC frame, a dashed replication link.
gap: Links from both app tiers to the cache, storage and NAT still run around the outside of the VPC (they now keep 12px apart where they used to touch). Shared services on the side (a column next to the zones) and merging of links that go to the same target with different labels would help.

title: Machine learning pipeline
context: Events are cleaned, turned into features, split, trained and evaluated; a good model is registered and deployed, a bad one goes back to tuning, and drift sends the pipeline round again.
uses: A decision, a loop back (retry), dashed feedback links, green and red outcomes, a dead end.
gap: A chain this long is folded into rows, and the feedback links (drift detected, new data) run the width of the page. Loops that return to the start of a pipeline need a way to be drawn as a short return, not a long line.

title: Support ticket triage
context: A ticket passes five questions on its way to being closed, answered from the knowledge base, paged or handled by an agent or engineering.
uses: `direction down`, a start and final state, decisions as pills, outcome colours.
gap: The lower half tangles: two links leave “needs engineering?” into the same box and a long link returns from the support agent. Decisions with two outcomes would be clearer if the layout put yes and no on opposite sides.

title: Home network
context: An ISP, a router, a switch and an access point with a dozen devices, a DNS filter and two backup links.
uses: `direction down` and nothing else; the fan-outs from the switch and the access point are merged into buses.
gap: Good. The backup links to the NAS cross the switch's bus, and the desktop is pushed to a second row because its link to the NAS is drawn below the switch's other devices.

title: CQRS with event sourcing
context: Commands append events to a store, a bus feeds a projector that updates a read model and three side effects; queries read the model.
uses: Three frames, dashed links, a link written backwards (query to client).
gap: Still a strip 1,600 px wide. The fold was tried (two rows) and rejected: it made the page-shaped version but with long return links (“orders”, “publish”) and more crossings. Writing the two sides as rows of frames by hand is what fixes it; the engine only folds when the result is no more tangled.

title: Build graph of a monorepo
context: Three apps, three feature packages and seven libraries, with who depends on whom.
uses: A dense graph with no layout help; the links into utils are merged into one bus.
gap: Readable, but busy: the middle of the diagram has twenty links in five columns, and arrowheads stack up on types and ui-kit.
